Title: Are Europe’s extreme summers the new normal? What the science says

nary_nodes.label: Last summer's heatwave caused 2,300 deaths
evidence: Last summer’s heatwave alone caused an estimated 2,300 climate-related deaths in 12 European countries, WWA says.

nary_nodes.label: Intense heat more likely now than in past
evidence: A study by World Weather Attribution (WWA) has found that intense heat on this level is now tens to hundreds of times more likely than it was in 2003, and was unheard of 50 years ago.

nary_nodes.label: Heat-related mortality to remain feature of warming climate
evidence: “Heat-related mortality is likely to remain a feature of Europe’s warming climate,” warns Dr Hans Kluge, the World Health Organization (WHO)’s regional director for Europe.

nary_nodes.label: Deaths rose by 52 per million annually since 1990s
evidence: Deaths have already risen by an average of 52 per million people annually since the 1990s, he told Al Jazeera – a trend he says shows little sign of reversing on its own.

“Heat-related mortality is likely to remain a feature of Europe’s warming climate,” warns Dr Hans Kluge, the World Health Organization (WHO)’s regional director for Europe. Deaths have already risen by an average of 52 per million people annually since the 1990s, he told Al Jazeera – a trend he says shows little sign of reversing on its own.

nary_nodes.label: Al Jazeera asks climate experts
evidence: We asked the climate experts:

Deaths have already risen by an average of 52 per million people annually since the 1990s, he told Al Jazeera – a trend he says shows little sign of reversing on its own. So what does this mean for the future? Are these temperatures the new normal, and if so, why? We asked the climate experts:

nary_nodes.label: Heatwaves were cooler in June 1976 and 2003
evidence: According to WWA, heatwaves were generally about 3.5C cooler in June 1976, and 2C cooler even in 2003.

nary_nodes.label: Global warming causes current heatwave conditions
evidence: Ultimately, this is down to global warming, he says.

“Think of it like a race where the starting line has been moved much closer to the finish,” Dr Akshay Deoras of the University of Reading told Al Jazeera. Ultimately, this is down to global warming, he says.

nary_nodes.label: Europe warmed at twice global average since 1980s
evidence: Europe has warmed at roughly twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Commission’s climate change service, Copernicus.

nary_nodes.label: Warming loads dice towards rare extremes
evidence: Deoras says this amounts to “loading the dice” towards once-rare extremes.

Europe has warmed at roughly twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Commission’s climate change service, Copernicus. Deoras says this amounts to “loading the dice” towards once-rare extremes.

nary_nodes.label: Heatwaves of this summer's magnitude expected every couple of decades
evidence: WWA’s modelling goes further: at current emissions rates, an event of the magnitude of this summer’s heatwave is expected to occur every couple of decades

nary_nodes.label: Today's extremes preview ordinary summer by mid-century
evidence: and today’s extremes are effectively a preview of what an ordinary summer could look like by the middle of the century.

nary_nodes.label: Heat dome traps heat
evidence: The immediate trigger is a stalled high-pressure system, or a “heat dome”, which traps heat in one concentrated area for days or weeks.

nary_nodes.label: Shifted baseline means heat domes produce hotter outcomes
evidence: Heat domes aren’t new, but Europe’s already-shifted baseline means the same pattern now produces far hotter outcomes than decades ago, Deoras told Al Jazeera.

nary_nodes.label: Warming from past emissions causes current extreme weather
evidence: Professor Hannah Cloke of the University of Reading told Al Jazeera that’s because the warming behind new, extreme weather patterns comes from emissions released decades ago, and the climate system takes time to respond – so we’re feeling the effects now of pollution from the past.

nary_nodes.label: 95% of Europe saw above-average temperatures last year
evidence: Copernicus’s European State of the Climate 2025 report confirms this: more than 95 percent of the continent saw above-average annual temperatures last year

Copernicus’s European State of the Climate 2025 report confirms this: more than 95 percent of the continent saw above-average annual temperatures last year, alongside record Alpine glacier loss and the highest sea-surface temperatures ever measured in Europe.

nary_nodes.label: Record Alpine glacier loss occurred last year
evidence: Copernicus’s European State of the Climate 2025 report confirms this: more than 95 percent of the continent saw above-average annual temperatures last year, alongside record Alpine glacier loss and the highest sea-surface temperatures ever measured in Europe.

nary_nodes.label: Highest sea-surface temperatures measured last year
evidence: Copernicus’s European State of the Climate 2025 report confirms this: more than 95 percent of the continent saw above-average annual temperatures last year, alongside record Alpine glacier loss and the highest sea-surface temperatures ever measured in Europe.

nary_nodes.label: Europe's warming gap with global average projected to widen
evidence: And because Europe is warming roughly twice as fast as the rest of the planet, that gap with the global average is projected to keep widening

nary_nodes.label: Europe will experience global average effects first and worse
evidence: meaning whatever the world experiences on average in the coming decades, Europe will likely see first, and worse.

nary_nodes.label: Some damage is permanent, some isn't yet
evidence: Partly. Some of the damage is permanent. Some of it isn’t – yet.

nary_nodes.label: Some effects of this summer are locked in
evidence: Because the effects of pollution from decades ago are cumulative, “some of what we are experiencing this summer is already locked in”, Cloke says.

nary_nodes.label: Alpine glaciers shrunk past recovery point
evidence: Alpine glaciers, which feed major European rivers, she says, have already shrunk past the point of recovery

Because the effects of pollution from decades ago are cumulative, “some of what we are experiencing this summer is already locked in”, Cloke says. Alpine glaciers, which feed major European rivers, she says, have already shrunk past the point of recovery

nary_nodes.label: Alpine glaciers' contribution to summer river flow permanently reduced
evidence: and their contribution to summer river flow is “permanently reduced”.
Alpine glaciers, which feed major European rivers, she says, have already shrunk past the point of recovery, and their contribution to summer river flow is “permanently reduced”.

nary_nodes.label: Avoiding emissions changes future odds
evidence: “Every tonne of emissions avoided changes the odds of what comes next,” Cloke says.

nary_nodes.label: Actions now decide future summer conditions
evidence: What we do now, therefore, will decide the difference between summers that are simply hard to live with in the future, and summers that become “genuinely beyond our ability to cope with”.

nary_nodes.label: Groundwater can recover, but window to act narrowing
evidence: Some resources, like groundwater in northern Europe, can still recover – “but the window to act is narrowing with each dry year”, she says.

“Every tonne of emissions avoided changes the odds of what comes next,” Cloke says. Some resources, like groundwater in northern Europe, can still recover – “but the window to act is narrowing with each dry year”, she says.

nary_nodes.label: 62,000 heat-related deaths in Europe in 2024
evidence: The Lancet Countdown Europe calculates that there were 62,000 heat-related deaths across the region in 2024 alone

nary_nodes.label: Heat-related deaths projected to rise steeply by 2050
evidence: with projections showing a steep further rise by 2050 if we don’t make changes.

nary_nodes.label: Architectural issues are major problem
evidence: Much of the problem, Kluge told Al Jazeera, is architectural and largely unaddressed.

nary_nodes.label: Housing stock designed for colder climate
evidence: “Most of the housing stock across this region was designed for a colder climate – to retain heat, not shed it,” he said

The Lancet Countdown Europe calculates that there were 62,000 heat-related deaths across the region in 2024 alone, with projections showing a steep further rise by 2050 if we don’t make changes. Much of the problem, Kluge told Al Jazeera, is architectural and largely unaddressed. “Most of the housing stock across this region was designed for a colder climate – to retain heat, not shed it,” he said

nary_nodes.label: Deaths could climb past 2050 without retrofitting
evidence: warning that without large-scale retrofitting, deaths could keep climbing past 2050 regardless of how good warning systems become.

nary_nodes.label: Governments need to plan for heat as predictable challenge
evidence: “Governments need to plan for heat the way they plan for winter flu – as a recurring, predictable challenge requiring permanent infrastructure, not a one-off crisis requiring emergency improvisation.”

nary_nodes.label: Identifying and reaching at-risk people is highest-return step
evidence: The highest-return step, he added, is identifying who’s most at risk – often older people living alone – and reaching them before a heatwave hits, not after.

nary_nodes.label: Early warning systems are priority
evidence: Cloke points to two priorities: early warning systems that reliably reach the people who most need to be protected

nary_nodes.label: Overhaul of water infrastructure is priority
evidence: Cloke points to two priorities: early warning systems that reliably reach the people who most need to be protected, and an overhaul of water infrastructure in Europe which has been built for rainfall patterns that no longer exist.

nary_nodes.label: Cutting emissions reduces heatwave intensity, frequency, duration
evidence: Deoras says emissions also still matter: cutting them won’t eliminate heatwaves, which are “a natural part of the climate system”, but doing so would make them “less intense, less frequent and shorter-lived”.

nary_nodes.label: Window of opportunity for addressing issue is narrowing
evidence: They do warn that the window of opportunity for addressing the issue is narrowing
None of the experts who spoke to Al Jazeera describe this as hopeless. They do warn that the window of opportunity for addressing the issue is narrowing

nary_nodes.label: Infrastructure, emissions, warning systems can be improved if decisions made now
evidence: infrastructure can still be retrofitted, emissions can still be cut, warning systems can still be improved – if the decisions to do so are made now, rather than after the next heatwave.

nary_nodes.label: Normal European summer in 2050 still being written
evidence: What a “normal” European summer looks like in 2050 is still being written, they say.
None of the experts who spoke to Al Jazeera describe this as hopeless. What a “normal” European summer looks like in 2050 is still being written, they say.
